readings.c1s4:
{{smaller block|<poem>There is a law in each ''well-order’d'' nation
To curb those raging appetites.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 180.}}}}

'''well-packing''' (wel′pak″ing), ''n.'' A cylindrical bag filled with flaxseed, or some similar apparatus, placed around the well-tube in deep oil-wells, to prevent the entrance of water above or below the oil in the well; a seed-bag. ''E. H. Knight.'' See cut under ''packing''.

'''well-pleasing''' (wel′plē′zing), ''a.'' Acceptable; pleasing.

{{smaller block|A sacrifice acceptable, ''well-pleasing'' to God.
{{right|Phil. iv. 18.}}}}

'''well-pleasing''' (wel′plē′zing), ''n.'' That which is well pleasing; also, the act of pleasing or satisfying. [Rare.]

432
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|The fruits of unity (next unto the ''well-pleasing'' of God, which is all in all) are two.
{{right|''Bacon'', Unity in Religion (ed. 1887).}}
Thou wouldst willingly walk in all ''well-pleasing'' unto Him.
{{right|''Bp. Leighton'', Com. on 1st Peter.}}}}

'''well-proportioned''' (wel′prọ̄-pōr′shọnd), ''a.'' Having good or correct proportions; fitting as to parts or relations; properly coördinated.

'''well-read''' (wel′red), ''a.'' Having read largely; having an extensive and intelligent knowledge of books or literature.

'''well-regulated''' (wel′reg′ū-lā-ted), ''a.'' Under proper regulation or control; in good order as to arrangement or management; well-ordered.
{{smaller block|Things which would have distressed most ''well-regulated'' Belgravian damsels.
{{right|''E. Yates'', Land at Last, iii. 3.}}}}

'''well-respected''' (wel′rē̤-spek′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Held in high respect; highly esteemed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>If ''well-respected'' honour bid me on,
I hold as little counsel with weak fear
As you, my lord.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 10.}}}}
'''2†.''' Having respect to facts or conditions; properly viewed; carefully weighed.

'''well-room''' (wel′röm), ''n.'' '''1.''' A room which contains a well; especially, a room built over a mineral spring, or into which its waters are conducted, and where they are drunk.—'''2.''' In a boat, a place in the bottom where leakage and rainwater are collected, to be thrown out with a scoop.

'''well-rounded''' (wel′roun′ded), ''a.'' Being well or properly rounded or filled out; symmetrically proportioned; complete in all parts.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''well-spoken''' (wel′spō″kn), ''a.'' '''1.''' Spoken well or with propriety: as, a ''well-spoken'' recitation. —'''2.''' See ''well spoken'', under ''speak''.

'''well-spring''' (wel′spring), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wellespring'', ''wilspring'', < AS. ''wyllspring'', ''wylspring'', a fountain, spring of water, < ''wyll'', well, + ''spring'', spring: see ''well''<sup>1</sup> and ''spring''.] '''1.''' A water-source; a fountainhead; a living spring. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|A litill brooke that com rennynge of two ''welle sprynges'' of a mountayne.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 338.}}}}
Hence —'''2.''' Figuratively, a perennial source of anything; a fountainhead of supply or of emanation.
{{smaller block|Understanding is a ''wellspring'' of life unto him that hath it.
{{right|Prov. xvi. 22.}}}}

'''well-staircase''' (wel′stãr″kās), ''n.'' A staircase forming or built around a well or well-hole. See ''well''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 5 (''a'').

'''well-sweep''' (wel′swēp), ''n.'' A sweep or pivoted pole to one end of which a bucket is hung for drawing water from a well.
{{smaller block|Leaning ''well-sweeps'' creaked in the scant garden.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 1.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''well-trap''' (wel′trap), ''n.'' Same as ''stink-trap.''

'''well-tube''' (wel′tūb), ''n.'' A wooden or metallic tube or piping running from top to bottom of a well for the fluid to rise or be pumped through. See cut under ''packing.''—{{smaller|'''Well-tube filter,''' a filter or strainer at the end of the tube of a driven well, to prevent the entrance of gravel or sand.}}

'''well-turned''' (wel′tėrnd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Accurately turned or rounded: as, a ''well-turned'' column.—'''2.''' Dexterously turned or fashioned; well-rounded; aptly constructed: as, a ''well-turned'' sentence or compliment.

'''well-warranted''' (wel′wor′ạn-ted), ''a.'' Having good warrant or credit; well-accredited; well-trusted.
{{smaller block|<poem>And you, my noble and ''well-warranted'' cousin, . . .
Do with your injuries as seems you best.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 254.}}}}

'''well-water''' (wel′wâ″tėr), ''n.'' The water of a well or of wells; water drawn from an artificial well.
{{smaller block|He alludes to the excellence of her freestone ''well-water,'' declares he must really take a third drink out of her nice gourd.
{{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 249.}}}}

'''well-willed†''', ''a.'' [< ME. ''welwyllyd''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''will''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Bearing good-will; favorable.

'''well-willer†''' (wel′wil″ėr), ''n.'' One who wills or wishes well; a well-wisher.
{{smaller block|[They] scornefullie mocke his worde, and also spitefullie hate and hurte all ''well willers'' thereof.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 82.}}
Be ruled by your ''well-willers.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 72.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|well-known|6877|well-wisher}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''well-known''' (wel′nōn), ''a.'' Fully or familiarly known; clearly apprehended; generally acknowledged.

<poem>Implored for aid each ''well-known'' face,
And strove to seek the Dame’s embrace.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iv. 25.}}}}

'''well-liking†''' (wel′lī″king), ''a.'' '''1.''' Appearing well; good-looking; well-conditioned.

{{smaller block|Children . . . as fat and as ''well-liking'' as if they had been gentlemen’s children. {{right|''Latimer.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Through the great providence of the Lord, they came all safe on shore, and most of them sound and ''well liking.''
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 244.}}}}

'''2.''' Showing off well; clever; smart.

{{smaller block|''Well-liking'' wits they have. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 268.}}}}

'''well-looked†''' (wel′lu̇kt), ''a.'' Well-looking; having a good appearance.

{{smaller block|They are both little, but very like one another, and ''well-looked'' children. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary, III. 270.}}}}

'''well-looking''' (wel′lu̇k″ing), ''a.'' Looking well; fairly good-looking.

{{smaller block|The horse was a bay, a ''well-looking'' animal enough.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
{{smaller block|She was a ''well-looking'', almost a handsome woman.
{{right|''J. C. Jeaffreson'', Live it Down, xxx.}}}}

'''well-mannered''' (wel′man″ėrd), ''a.''   [< ME. ''well maneryd''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''mannered.'']   Having good manners; polite; well-bred; complaisant.

{{smaller block|Sir, if you will not that men call you presumptuous, or, to speake plainly, do call you foole, haue a care to be ''well manered.''
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 74.}}}}

'''well-marked''' (wel′märkt), ''a.'' '''1.''' In ''zoöl.'' and ''bot.'', pronounced; decided; obvious; signal; easily recognized or determined: as, ''well-marked'' characters; a ''well-marked'' genus, species, or variety.—'''2.''' Specifying a South African tortoise, ''Homopus signatus. P. L. Sclater.''

'''well-meaner''' (wel′mē′nėr), ''n.'' One who means well, or whose intention is good.
{{smaller block|Deluded ''well-meaners'' come over out of honesty, and small offenders out of common discretion or fear.
{{right|''Dryden'', Vind. of Duke of Guise.}}}}

'''well-meaning''' (wel′mē′ning), ''a.'' Well-intentioned: frequently used with slight contempt.
{{smaller block|Plain ''well-meaning'' soul. {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 128.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was ever a timorous, chicken-spirited, though ''well-meaning'' man. {{right|''Scott'', Fair Maid of Perth, xx.}}}}

'''well-meant''' (wel′ment), ''a.'' Rightly intended; friendly; sincere; not feigned.
{{smaller block|Edward’s ''well-meant'' honest love.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 3. 67.}}}}

'''well-minded''' (wel′mīn′ded), ''a.'' Of good or well-disposed mind; well or favorably inclined.
{{smaller block|For discharge of a bishop’s office, to be ''well-minded'' is not enough. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, vii. 24.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Well-minded'' Clarence, be thou fortunate!
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 8. 27.}}}}

'''well-natured''' (wel′nā′t̮ṳ̄rd), ''a.'' Of excellent nature or character; properly disposed; right-minded.
{{smaller block|<poem>On their life no grievous burthen lies,
Who are ''well-natured'', temperate, and wise.</poem>
{{right|''Sir J. Denham'', Old Age.}}}}
{{smaller block|They shou’d rather disturb than divert the ''well-natur’d'' and reflecting Part of an Audience.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, Ded.}}}}

'''wellness''' (wel′nes), ''n.''   [< ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ness''.]   The state of being well or in good health.   ''Hood.''

'''well-nigh''' (wel′nī′), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wel ny'', ''wel nygh'', ''wel neih''; prop. two words: see ''well''<sup>2</sup> and ''nigh''.]   Very nigh; very nearly; almost wholly or entirely. Also written as a single word and (more properly) as two words.
{{smaller block|<poem>A wegge of boone or yron putte bytwene
The bark and tree ''welnygh'' III fingers depe.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 73.}}}}
{{smaller block|The labour of ''wel-nigh'' fifty pioners.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|The dreary night has ''wellnigh'' passed.
{{right|''Whittier'', Pæan.}}}}

'''well-ordered''' (wel′ôr′dėrd), ''a.'' Rightly or correctly ordered, regulated, or governed.
<poem>There is a law in each ''well-order’d'' nation
To curb those raging appetites.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 180.}}}}

'''well-pleasing''' (wel′plē′zing), ''a.'' Acceptable; pleasing.

{{smaller block|A sacrifice acceptable, ''well-pleasing'' to God.
{{right|Phil. iv. 18.}}}}

'''well-pleasing''' (wel′plē′zing), ''n.'' That which is well pleasing; also, the act of pleasing or satisfying. [Rare.]

432 {{smaller block|The fruits of unity (next unto the ''well-pleasing'' of God, which is all in all) are two.
{{right|''Bacon'', Unity in Religion (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou wouldst willingly walk in all ''well-pleasing'' unto Him.
{{right|''Bp. Leighton'', Com. on 1st Peter.}}}}

'''well-proportioned''' (wel′prọ̄-pōr′shọnd), ''a.'' Having good or correct proportions; fitting as to parts or relations; properly coördinated.

'''well-read''' (wel′red), ''a.'' Having read largely; having an extensive and intelligent knowledge of books or literature.

'''well-regulated''' (wel′reg′ū-lā-ted), ''a.'' Under proper regulation or control; in good order as to arrangement or management; well-ordered.
{{smaller block|Things which would have distressed most ''well-regulated'' Belgravian damsels.
{{right|''E. Yates'', Land at Last, iii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>If ''well-respected'' honour bid me on,
I hold as little counsel with weak fear
As you, my lord.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 10.}}}}
'''2†.''' Having respect to facts or conditions; properly viewed; carefully weighed.

'''well-room''' (wel′röm), ''n.'' '''1.''' A room which contains a well; especially, a room built over a mineral spring, or into which its waters are conducted, and where they are drunk.—'''2.''' In a boat, a place in the bottom where leakage and rainwater are collected, to be thrown out with a scoop.

'''well-rounded''' (wel′roun′ded), ''a.'' Being well or properly rounded or filled out; symmetrically proportioned; complete in all parts. {{smaller block|Something so complete and ''well-rounded'' in his . . . life.{{right|''Longfellow.''}}}}

'''well-seen†''' (wel′sēn′), ''a.'' Highly accomplished; expert; skilful.
{{smaller block|All sixe ''well-seene'' in armes, and prov’d in many a fight.{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As a schoolmaster
''Well seen'' in music, to instruct Bianca.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 2. 134.}}}}

'''well-set''' (wel′set′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Firmly set or fixed; properly placed or arranged.
{{smaller block|Instead of a girdle, a rent; and, instead of ''well set'' hair, baldness.{{right|Isa. iii. 24.}}}}
'''2.''' Symmetrically formed; properly joined or put together: as, a ''well-set'' frame or body.

'''well-sinker''' (wel′sing″kėr), ''n.'' One who sinks or digs wells.
{{smaller block|Modern ''well-sinkers'' will go down in any strata almost to any depth.{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LV. 89.}}}}

'''well-sinking''' (wel′sing″king), ''n.'' The operation of sinking or digging wells; the act of boring for water.

'''well-smack''' (wel′smak), ''n.'' A fishing-smack furnished with a well; a smack. [Canada and New Eng.]

'''well-spherometer''' (wel′sfē-rom″e-tėr), ''n.'' A form of spherometer for accurately measuring the radius of curvature of a lens.

'''well-spoken''' (wel′spō″kn), ''a.'' '''1.''' Spoken well or with propriety: as, a ''well-spoken'' recitation. —'''2.''' See ''well spoken'', under ''speak''.

'''well-spring''' (wel′spring), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wellespring'', ''wilspring'', < AS. ''wyllspring'', ''wylspring'', a fountain, spring of water, < ''wyll'', well, + ''spring'', spring: see ''well''<sup>1</sup> and ''spring''.]   '''1.''' A water-source; a fountainhead; a living spring. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|A litill brooke that com rennynge of two ''welle sprynges'' of a mountayne.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 338.}}}}
Hence —'''2.''' Figuratively, a perennial source of anything; a fountainhead of supply or of emanation.
{{smaller block|Understanding is a ''wellspring'' of life unto him that hath it.
{{right|Prov. xvi. 22.}}}}

'''well-staircase''' (wel′stãr″kās), ''n.'' A staircase forming or built around a well or well-hole. See ''well''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 5 (''a'').

'''well-sweep''' (wel′swēp), ''n.'' A sweep or pivoted pole to one end of which a bucket is hung for drawing water from a well.
{{smaller block|Leaning ''well-sweeps'' creaked in the scant garden.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 1.}}}}

'''well-tempered''' (wel′tem′pėrd), ''a.'' In ''music,'' tuned in equal temperament. {{smaller|The term is used specifically in the (English) title of one of J. S. Bach’s most famous works, “The Well-Tempered Clavichord,” a collection of forty-eight preludes and fugues, in two equal parts, one finished in 1722 and the other in 1744, which were written in all the major and minor keys (tonalities) of the keyboard for the purpose of testing the theory of tuning in equal temperament, at that time but little known. See ''temperament.''}}

'''well-thewed''' (wel′thūd), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wel-thewed, wel thewed;'' < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''thewed.'']   Good in manner, habit, form, or construction; well-mannered; well done.
<poem>They bene so ''well-thewed'', and so wise,
What ever that good old man bespake.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., February.}}}}

'''well-timbered''' (wel′tim′bėrd), ''a.'' Well furnished with timber: as, ''well-timbered'' land; also, made with good or abundant timber, literally or figuratively; strongly formed or built.
{{smaller block|A ''well-timbered'' fellow, he would have made a good column, an he had been thought on when the house was a building.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, Ind.}}}}

'''well-timed''' (wel′tīmd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Done at a good or suitable time; opportune.
{{smaller block|Methinks an angry scorn is here ''well-timed.''
{{right|''Lowell'', To G. W. Curtis.}}}}
'''2.''' Keeping accurate time: as, ''well-timed'' oars.

'''well-to-do''' (wel′tọ̈-dö′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having means to do or get along with; well off; forehanded; prosperous: as, a ''well-to-do'' merchant or farmer.
{{smaller block|I am rich and ''well-to-do.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}
'''2.''' Manifesting a state of being well off; indicative of prosperity.
{{smaller block|There was a ''well-to-do'' aspect about the place.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Tobermory is a commonplace town, with a semicircle of ''well-to-do'' houses on the shores of a sheltered bay.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVII. 498.}}}}

'''well-tomb''' (wel′töm), ''n.'' A deeply excavated tomb; one of a numerous class of ancient burial-pits, as in Egypt and in Phenician lands, etc., sunk in the ground or rock like wells.
{{smaller block|The graves belong to the type of ''well-tombs'', and show a curious and subtle art in their design for the purposes of concealment.
{{right|''The Nation'', XLVIII. 303.}}}}

'''well-trap''' (wel′trap), ''n.'' Same as ''stink-trap.''

'''well-tube''' (wel′tūb), ''n.'' A wooden or metallic tube or piping running from top to bottom of a well for the fluid to rise or be pumped through. See cut under ''packing.''—{{smaller|'''Well-tube filter,''' a filter or strainer at the end of the tube of a driven well, to prevent the entrance of gravel or sand.}}

'''well-turned''' (wel′tėrnd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Accurately turned or rounded: as, a ''well-turned'' column.—'''2.''' Dexterously turned or fashioned; well-rounded; aptly constructed: as, a ''well-turned'' sentence or compliment.

'''well-warranted''' (wel′wor′ạn-ted), ''a.'' Having good warrant or credit; well-accredited; well-trusted.
{{smaller block|<poem>And you, my noble and ''well-warranted'' cousin, . . .
Do with your injuries as seems you best.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 254.}}}}

'''well-water''' (wel′wâ″tėr), ''n.'' The water of a well or of wells; water drawn from an artificial well.
{{smaller block|He alludes to the excellence of her freestone ''well-water,'' declares he must really take a third drink out of her nice gourd.
{{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 249.}}}}

'''well-willed†''', ''a.''   [< ME. ''welwyllyd''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''will''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Bearing good-will; favorable.

'''well-willer†''' (wel′wil″ėr), ''n.'' One who wills or wishes well; a well-wisher.
{{smaller block|[They] scornefullie mocke his worde, and also spitefullie hate and hurte all ''well willers'' thereof.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 82.}}}}
{{smaller block|Be ruled by your ''well-willers.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 72.}}}}

'''well-willing†''' (wel′wil″ing), ''a.''   [< ME. ''welewyllyng, welwillende,'' < AS. ''welwillende'' (tr. L. ''benevolus''), < ''wel,'' well, + ''willende,'' ppr. of ''will''<sup>1</sup>.]   Wishing well; well-inclined; favorable; friendly; propitious.
{{smaller block|<poem>To ther desire the kyng was ''welewillyng,''
So fourth on huntyng he rode certeynly.</poem>{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 964.}}}}

'''well-willy†''' (wel′wil″i), ''a.''   [Also ''wel-willy''; Sc. ''weill-willie''; < ME. ''wellwilly'' (= Sw. ''välvillig'' = Dan. ''velvillig''), benevolent; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''will''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''well-willing.'']   Kindly wishing; favorable; propitious.
{{smaller block|<poem>Venus mene I, the ''welwilly'' planete.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1257.}}}}

'''well-wish†''' (wel′wish′), ''n.'' A good or favorable wish; a benevolent desire.
{{smaller block|If this be true, I must confess I am charitable only in my liberal intentions, and bountiful ''well-wishes.''
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, ii. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let it not . . . enter into the heart of any one that hath . . . a ''well-wish'' for his friends or posterity to think of a peace with France.
{{right|''Addison'', Present State of the War.}}}}

'''well-wished†''' (wel′wisht), ''a.'' Held in good will; highly esteemed; well-liked.
{{smaller block|<poem>The general, subject to a ''well-wish’d'' king,
Quit their own part. ''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 4. 27.</poem>}}

'''well-wisher''' (wel′wish′ėr), ''n.'' One who wishes well, as to a person or a cause; a person favorably inclined; a sympathizing friend.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
